claim: In the ant Lasius neglectus, fungal infections (Metarhizium brunneum) can be mitigated by employing an efficient multicomponent behaviour termed destructive disinfection.
source: Here, we show that in a social insect, the ant Lasius neglectus, the negative consequences of fungal infections (Metarhizium brunneum) can be mitigated by employing an efficient multicomponent behaviour, termed destructive disinfection, which prevents further spread of the disease through the colony.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that ants perform destructive disinfection behaviors that prevent pathogen replication and disease spread.

claim: Destructive disinfection prevents further spread of disease through the colony.
source: Here, we show that in a social insect, the ant Lasius neglectus, the negative consequences of fungal infections (Metarhizium brunneum) can be mitigated by employing an efficient multicomponent behaviour, termed destructive disinfection, which prevents further spread of the disease through the colony.
evidence: Experimental data in Figure 4A shows no disease transmission from destructively disinfected pupae.

claim: Ants specifically target infected pupae during the pathogen's non-contagious incubation period.
source: Ants specifically target infected pupae during the pathogen's non-contagious incubation period, utilising chemical 'sickness cues' emitted by pupae.
evidence: Data shows that unpacking occurred 2-10 days after pathogen exposure, and 85% of unpacked pupae harbored infections (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: Ants utilize chemical 'sickness cues' emitted by pupae to detect infections.
source: Ants specifically target infected pupae during the pathogen's non-contagious incubation period, utilising chemical 'sickness cues' emitted by pupae.
evidence: Chemical analysis showed distinct CHC profiles on infected pupae, and pentane washing reduced unpacking by 72% (Figure 2).

claim: Ants remove the pupal cocoon, perforate its cuticle and administer antimicrobial poison during destructive disinfection.
source: They then remove the pupal cocoon, perforate its cuticle and administer antimicrobial poison, which enters the body and prevents pathogen replication from the inside out.
evidence: Behavioral observations and in vitro experiments demonstrate these three components are necessary for pathogen inhibition (Figure 1, Figure 3).

claim: The antimicrobial poison enters the body and prevents pathogen replication from the inside out.
source: They then remove the pupal cocoon, perforate its cuticle and administer antimicrobial poison, which enters the body and prevents pathogen replication from the inside out.
evidence: In vitro experiments showed that all three components (unpacking, biting, poison) are required to prevent sporulation (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: Ants destroy infected brood to stop the pathogen completing its lifecycle, thus protecting the rest of the colony.
source: Like the immune system of a metazoan body that specifically targets and eliminates infected cells, ants destroy infected brood to stop the pathogen completing its lifecycle, thus protecting the rest of the colony.
evidence: Data shows that destructive disinfection prevented pathogen sporulation and disease transmission (Figure 3A, Figure 4A).

claim: The same principles of disease defence apply at different levels of biological organisation (metazoan bodies and ant colonies).
source: Hence, in an analogous fashion, the same principles of disease defence apply at different levels of biological organisation.
evidence: The manuscript draws parallels between immune cell elimination of infected cells and ant elimination of infected brood, based on logical comparison.

claim: Social animals are expected to experience a greater risk of disease outbreaks than solitary species because their higher number of within-group interactions will promote pathogen spread.
source: Social animals are therefore expected to experience a greater risk of disease outbreaks than solitary species, because their higher number of within-group interactions will promote pathogen spread (Nunn and Altizer, 2006; Schmid-Hempel, 2017; Alexander, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on disease ecology in social animals.

claim: Traits mitigating the cost of disease should have been selected for in group-living animals as an essential adaptation to social life.
source: As a consequence, evolutionary immunology predicts that traits mitigating this cost, such as detecting sick conspecifics and using that information to prevent self-infection, should have been selected for in group-living animals as an essential adaptation to social life (Hamilton, 1987; Ezenwa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from evolutionary immunology supported by citations.

claim: Social animals including lobsters, tadpoles, mice and mandrills can use conspicuous disease-associated changes in the physical appearance, behaviour and chemical odour of conspecifics to identify sick group members.
source: Social animals, including lobsters, tadpoles, mice and mandrills, can use conspicuous disease-associated changes in the physical appearance, behaviour and chemical odour of conspecifics to identify sick group members (Shakhar and Shakhar, 2015; Arakawa et al., 2011; Lopes, 2014; Bozza, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on disease detection in various social animals.

claim: Upon detection of sick conspecifics, healthy animals usually respond by interacting with sick conspecifics less or avoiding them completely.
source: Upon detection, healthy animals usually respond by interacting with sick conspecifics less or avoiding them completely (Poirotte et al., 2017; Kiesecker et al., 1999; Behringer et al., 2006; Anderson and Behringer, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies documenting avoidance behaviors.

claim: Healthy animals may prophylactically increase the expression of their immune defences in preparation for a potential immune challenge when detecting sick conspecifics.
source: In addition, they may prophylactically increase the expression of their immune defences in preparation for a potential immune challenge (Hernández López et al., 2017), and a similar phenomenon is observed in animals and plants in response to chemicals released by wounded conspecifics (Heil and Silva Bueno, 2007; Peuß et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on prophylactic immune upregulation.

claim: Sick animals may attempt to hide their illness under some circumstances because there are downsides to being socially excluded.
source: Because there are downsides to being socially excluded, sick animals may, under some circumstances, attempt to hide their illness (Lopes, 2014; Lopes et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on sickness behavior.

claim: Signalling infection to others should be adaptive if this elicits care from conspecifics that improves the chance of recovery.
source: However, signalling infection to others should be adaptive if (i) this elicits care from conspecifics that improves the chance of recovery (Hart, 1990) or (ii) if the infection is otherwise likely to spread and infect kin (Shakhar and Shakhar, 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citations to evolutionary biology literature.

claim: Signalling infection to others should be adaptive if the infection is otherwise likely to spread and infect kin.
source: However, signalling infection to others should be adaptive if (i) this elicits care from conspecifics that improves the chance of recovery (Hart, 1990) or (ii) if the infection is otherwise likely to spread and infect kin (Shakhar and Shakhar, 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on kin selection theory, supported by citation.

claim: In closely related social groups, there may be selection for both the detection of illnesses by healthy group members and the advertisement of an animal's disease status by sick individuals themselves.
source: Hence, in closely related social groups, there may be selection for both the detection of illnesses by healthy group members (Curtis, 2014) and the advertisement of an animal's disease status by sick individuals themselves (Shakhar and Shakhar, 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on inclusive fitness theory, supported by citations.

claim: Social insect colonies are typically single families, comprised of a queen and her daughters, the workers.
source: In the social insects (termites and ants and the social bees and wasps), colonies are typically single families, comprised of a queen and her daughters, the workers (Queller and Strassmann, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about social insect biology, supported by citation.

claim: Social insect colonies have an irreversible reproductive division of labour, with queens and workers being highly interdependent.
source: They typically have an irreversible reproductive division of labour, with the two castes being highly interdependent: the queens are morphologically specialised for reproduction and cannot survive without the assistance of the workers; conversely, the workers cannot reproduce, but gain fitness indirectly by raising the queen's offspring (Queller and Strassmann, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about social insect biology, supported by citation.

claim: Social insect societies have become indivisible, reproductive units, where natural selection acts on the colony instead of its individual members.
source: Consequently, social insect societies have become indivisible, reproductive units, where natural selection acts on the colony instead of its individual members (Bourke, 2011; West et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical concept in evolutionary biology supported by citations.

claim: Social insect colonies are often termed 'superorganisms' and their emergence is considered a major evolutionary transition.
source: Hence, social insect colonies are often termed 'superorganisms' and their emergence is considered a major evolutionary transition (Bourke, 2011; West et al., 2015; Wheeler, 1911; Boomsma and Gawne, 2017).
evidence: This is established terminology and theory in evolutionary biology, supported by citations.

claim: Social insects have evolved physiological and behavioural adaptations that limit the colony-level impact of infectious diseases.
source: In particular, social insects have evolved physiological and behavioural adaptations that limit the colony-level impact of infectious diseases, which could otherwise spread easily due to the intimate social interactions between colony members (Cremer et al., 2007; Rosengaus et al., 2011; Boomsma et al., 2005; Cremer et al., 2017; Stroeymeyt et al., 2014; Meunier, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about social immunity, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Social immunity is an emergent layer of protection performed collectively by workers that protects the colony from invading pathogens, like the immune system of a body.
source: These defences are performed collectively by the workers to form an emergent layer of protection known as social immunity that, like the immune system of a body, protects the colony from invading pathogens (Cremer et al., 2007; Rosengaus et al., 2011; Cremer et al., 2017; Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
evidence: This is an established concept in social insect biology, supported by citations.

claim: Sanitary care in ants involves grooming and the use of antimicrobial secretions to mechanically remove and chemically disinfect pathogens.
source: In ants, sanitary care involves grooming and the use of antimicrobial secretions to mechanically remove and chemically disinfect pathogens, reducing the likelihood that pathogen exposure leads to the development of an infection (Tragust et al., 2013a; Graystock and Hughes, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ant sanitary care, supported by citations.

claim: Social immunity is characterised by a care-kill dichotomy, where colony members should be cared for when possible but sacrificed if necessary.
source: Hence, social immunity is characterised by a care-kill dichotomy, where colony members should be cared for when possible but sacrificed if necessary, both of which benefit the colony (Cremer et al., 2017; Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework for understanding social immunity, supported by citations.

claim: The kill-component is a unique feature of social immunity that is not present in the disease defence repertoire of other forms of sociality.
source: Although the kill-component is an unique feature of social immunity that is not present in the disease defence repertoire of other forms of sociality (e.g. non-superorganismal family groups, communal breeders or aggregations [Cremer et al., 2017]), it is rarely studied in comparison to the care-component.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the uniqueness of social immunity, supported by citation.

claim: What happens when sanitary care fails and a pathogen successfully infects a colony member remains poorly understood.
source: Hence, what happens when sanitary care fails and a pathogen successfully infects a colony member, with the consequent potential to create an epidemic, remains poorly understood (but see [Rothenbuhler, 1964; Ugelvig et al., 2010; Tragust et al., 2013b]).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge, with citations to limited prior work.

claim: Infections should be detected quickly and accurately by nestmates to overcome the pathogen before it has time to replicate and produce propagules that can infect others.
source: To effectively protect the colony, we predict that infections should be detected quickly and accurately by nestmates, in order to overcome the pathogen before it has time to replicate and produce propagules that can infect others.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on theoretical reasoning about effective disease control.

claim: The colony should respond by eliminating the infection as effectively as possible, by preventing any further opportunities for disease transmission.
source: Once detected, the colony should respond by eliminating the infection as effectively as possible, by preventing any further opportunities for disease transmission.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on theoretical reasoning about effective disease control.

claim: Fungus-infected ants become highly contagious to nestmates after death and can cause epidemics that result in colony collapse.
source: For example, previous studies have shown that fungus-infected ants become highly contagious to nestmates after death and can cause epidemics that result in colony collapse (Hughes et al., 2002; Loreto and Hughes, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When Metarhizium infectious conidiospores come into contact with insect cuticle, they attach, germinate and penetrate the host cuticle within 24–48 hr to cause internal infections.
source: When the infectious conidiospores of this fungus come into contact with insect cuticle, they attach, germinate and penetrate the host cuticle within 24–48 hr to cause internal infections (Vestergaard et al., 1999; Walker and Hughes, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Metarhizium infection biology, supported by citations.

claim: During a short, non-infectious incubation period following Metarhizium infection, the fungus goes through a single-cell blastospore stage, which lasts 1–2 days.
source: During a short, non-infectious incubation period following infection, the fungus goes through a single-cell blastospore stage, which lasts 1–2 days.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Metarhizium lifecycle.

claim: Once the host has died from Metarhizium infection, the fungus enters a saprophytic mycelial phase, then grows out of the corpse 1–3 days later, releasing millions of new infectious conidiospores in a process called sporulation.
source: Once the host has died, the fungus enters a saprophytic mycelial phase, then grows out of the corpse, 1–3 days later, releasing millions of new infectious conidiospores, in a process called sporulation (Hughes et al., 2002; Deacon, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Metarhizium lifecycle, supported by citations.

claim: Brood infected with Metarhizium is removed from the brood chamber.
source: Previous work found that brood infected with Metarhizium is removed from the brood chamber (Ugelvig et al., 2010; Tragust et al., 2013b), however, it is unknown how the ants then respond to the infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ants tending pathogen-exposed pupae prematurely removed the pupae from their cocoons in a behaviour termed 'unpacking', whereas control pupae were left cocooned.
source: We observed that ants tending pathogen-exposed pupae prematurely removed the pupae from their cocoons in a behaviour we termed 'unpacking', whereas control pupae were left cocooned (Figure 1A–B, Video 1; Cox proportional hazards regression: likelihood ratio test (LR) χ2= 55.48, df = 3, p<0.001; hazard ratios (x greater chance of unpacking compared to control): low dose = 18, medium = 53, high = 111; post-hoc comparisons: control vs. low, p=0.004; low vs. medium, p=0.006; medium vs. high = 0.024; all others, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1A-B and Video 1.

claim: Unpacking occurred between 2 and 10 days after pathogen exposure, but sooner and more frequently at higher conidiospore dosages.
source: Unpacking occurred between 2 and 10 days after pathogen exposure, but sooner and more frequently at higher conidiospore dosages (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ants were unable to remove any conidiospores from the majority of the cocoons or the unpacked pupae at the time of unpacking.
source: As unpacking was a belated response to pathogen exposure and we were unable to remove any conidiospores from the majority of the cocoons or the unpacked pupae (number of colony forming units [mean ± 95% CIs]: cocoons = 0.6 ± 0.9; pupae = 0.1 ± 0.35; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we concluded that the ants were not performing unpacking to simply dispose of contaminated cocoons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on CFU counts shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: On average across the conidiospore dosages, 85% of unpacked pupae harboured infections that sporulated in the absence of the ants.
source: We found that, on average across the conidiospore dosages, 85% of unpacked pupae harboured infections that sporulated in the absence of the ants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from incubation experiments.

claim: Only 25% of non-unpacked pupae were infected.
source: In contrast, only 25% of non-unpacked pupae were infected (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; generalised linear model [GLM]: overall LR χ2 = 26.48, df = 5, p<0.001; cocooned vs. unpacked pupae: LR χ2 = 18.5, df = 1, p=0.001; conidiospore dose: LR χ2 = 0.42, df = 2, p=0.81).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ants were detecting and unpacking pupae with lethal infections during the asymptomatic incubation period of the pathogen's lifecycle.
source: We therefore concluded that the ants were detecting and unpacking pupae with lethal infections during the asymptomatic incubation period of the pathogen's lifecycle.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that unpacked pupae had high infection rates and unpacking occurred before external symptoms.

claim: At the time of unpacking, the fungus growing inside the pupae is non-infectious and essentially no viable conidiospores are leftover from the pathogen exposure on their cuticle.
source: At this time point, the fungus growing inside the pupae is non-infectious and essentially no viable conidiospores are leftover from the pathogen exposure on their cuticle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), so there is very little risk of the ants contracting the disease whilst unpacking the pupae.
evidence: This is supported by CFU data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and knowledge of fungal lifecycle.

claim: After unpacking, the ants sprayed the pupae with poison from their acidopore approximately 15-times more frequently than during sanitary care.
source: The ants sprayed the pupae with poison from their acidopore approx. 15-times more frequently than during sanitary care (~13 times/d; Figure 1D; generalised linear mixed model [GLMM]: LR χ2 = 17.04, df = 1, p<0.001), and grooming duration doubled (Figure 1C; linear mixed effects regression [LMER]: LR χ2 = 145.26, df = 1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Grooming duration doubled after unpacking compared to sanitary care.
source: The ants sprayed the pupae with poison from their acidopore approx. 15-times more frequently than during sanitary care (~13 times/d; Figure 1D; generalised linear mixed model [GLMM]: LR χ2 = 17.04, df = 1, p<0.001), and grooming duration doubled (Figure 1C; linear mixed effects regression [LMER]: LR χ2 = 145.26, df = 1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The ants repeatedly bit the pupae to make perforations in their cuticles and to remove their limbs after unpacking.
source: Furthermore, the ants repeatedly bit the pupae to make perforations in their cuticles and to remove their limbs (Figure 1E; GLMM: LR χ2 = 39.44, df = 1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observation data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The combination of unpacking, grooming, poison spraying and biting resulted in the death of the pupae and left their corpses heavily damaged and coated in the ants' poison.
source: Together these three behaviours resulted in the death of the pupae and left their corpses heavily damaged and coated in the ants' poison (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by observational data and measurements shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Pentane-washed pupae showed a 72% reduction in unpacking compared to both non- and water-washed infected pupae.
source: We washed infected pupae in pentane to reduce the abundance of their cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs). When pentane-washed pupae were presented to ants, there was a 72% reduction in unpacking compared to both non- and water-washed infected pupae (Figure 2A; GLM: LR χ2 = 12.2, df = 2, p=0.002; Tukey post hoc comparisons: water-washed vs. non-washed, p=0.79; all others, p=0.009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Pentane-washed pupae had lower abundances of CHCs.
source: As pentane-washed pupae had lower abundances of CHCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), this result indicates that the ants use one or more cuticular compounds to detect the infections.
evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ants use one or more cuticular compounds to detect the infections.
source: As pentane-washed pupae had lower abundances of CHCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), this result indicates that the ants use one or more cuticular compounds to detect the infections.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the pentane washing experiment showing reduced unpacking when CHCs are removed.

claim: Unpacked pathogen-exposed pupae have distinct chemical profiles compared to sham-treated control pupae.
source: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis of the solvent wash confirmed that unpacked pupae have distinct chemical profiles compared to non-infected control pupae, whilst cocooned (non-unpacked) pathogen-exposed pupae were intermediate (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2; perMANOVA: F = 1.49, df = 46, p=0.002; post-hoc perMANOVA comparisons: unpacked vs. control, p=0.003; unpacked vs. cocooned, p=0.79; cocooned vs. control, p=0.08).
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS chemical analysis data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: There were no novel compounds present on unpacked or cocooned pathogen-exposed pupae that were not also present on control pupae.
source: There were no novel compounds present on unpacked or cocooned pathogen-exposed pupae that were not also present on control pupae (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these differences were not caused by odours emitted directly by the fungus, but were of pupal origin.
evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The chemical differences on infected pupae were not caused by odours emitted directly by the fungus, but were of pupal origin.
source: There were no novel compounds present on unpacked or cocooned pathogen-exposed pupae that were not also present on control pupae (Table 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these differences were not caused by odours emitted directly by the fungus, but were of pupal origin.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the absence of novel compounds and confirmed by direct comparison of fungal and pupal chemical profiles.

claim: There were no fungus-derived peaks in the pupal chemical profiles.
source: By analysing the chemical profiles of each of the pathogen's separate developmental stages (infectious conidiospores, post-infection blastospores, and saprophytic mycelium) and performing a direct comparison of the fungal compounds to the pupal chemical profiles, we confirmed that there were no fungus-derived peaks in the pupal profiles (see Materials and methods for more information).
evidence: This is supported by comparative chemical analysis of fungal and pupal profiles.

claim: Eight out of the 24 CHCs identified had higher relative abundances on unpacked pupae compared to control pupae.
source: Correspondingly, we found that 8 out of the 24 CHCs identified (Table 1) had higher relative abundances on unpacked pupae compared to control pupae (Figure 2C–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2; all Kruskal-Wallis [KW] test statistics and post-hoc comparisons in Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data and statistical analysis, with reference to figures and tables.

claim: Four CHCs were present in relatively higher quantities on unpacked pupae compared to the non-unpacked cocooned pupae.
source: Moreover, four of these CHCs were also present in relatively higher quantities on unpacked pupae compared to the non-unpacked cocooned pupae.
evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data shown in Table 2 and Figure 2C-F.

claim: Several specific CHCs are probably accumulating on infected pupae over time, eventually reaching an amount that is sufficient to elicit destructive disinfection.
source: Several specific CHCs are therefore probably accumulating on infected pupae over time, eventually reaching an amount that, relative to the other compounds, is sufficient to elicit destructive disinfection. This corresponds to current models of social insect behaviour, where the likelihood of a response depends on stimuli exceeding a certain threshold (Theraulaz et al., 1998; Beshers and Fewell, 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing dose-dependent unpacking and CHC accumulation, combined with theoretical models cited.

claim: PGRP-SC2 showed increased gene expression 48 hr after β-glucan injection, compared to pupae immediately after injection.
source: However, both (B) PGRP-SC2, an IMD pathway regulator gene (Bischoff et al., 2006), and (C) β−1,3-GBP, a pattern recognition protein that specifically binds to fungal β-glucans (Ma and Kanost, 2000; Gottar et al., 2006), showed increased gene expression 48 hr after injection, compared to pupae immediately after injection (PGRP-SC2: U = 17, p=0.0095; β−1,3-GBP: U = 19, p=0.01), but not following saline injection (PGRP-SC2: U = 70, p=0.06; β−1,3-GBP, saline: U = 81, p=0.0095, a significant down regulation).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: β−1,3-GBP showed increased gene expression 48 hr after β-glucan injection, compared to pupae immediately after injection.
source: However, both (B) PGRP-SC2, an IMD pathway regulator gene (Bischoff et al., 2006), and (C) β−1,3-GBP, a pattern recognition protein that specifically binds to fungal β-glucans (Ma and Kanost, 2000; Gottar et al., 2006), showed increased gene expression 48 hr after injection, compared to pupae immediately after injection (PGRP-SC2: U = 17, p=0.0095; β−1,3-GBP: U = 19, p=0.01), but not following saline injection (PGRP-SC2: U = 70, p=0.06; β−1,3-GBP, saline: U = 81, p=0.0095, a significant down regulation).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Pupae injected with β−1,3-glucans had increased relative abundances of Tritriacontadiene (C33:2) 2 days after injection compared to pupae immediately after injection.
source: Pupae injected with β−1,3-glucans (green dots) had increased relative abundances 2 days after injection compared to pupae immediately after injection, of (A) Tritriacontadiene, C33:2 (LMER: LR χ2 = x, df = 1, p=0.012) and (B) Tritriacontene, C33:1 (LR χ2 = 6.40, df = 1, p=0.046), but not (C) Pentatriacontadiene, C35:2 (LR χ2 = 1.56, df = 1, p=0.42) or (D) co-eluting Pentatriacontadiene and Pentatriacontene, C35:2 + C35:1 (LR χ2 = 0.25, df = 1, p=0.70).
evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Pupae injected with β−1,3-glucans had increased relative abundances of Tritriacontene (C33:1) 2 days after injection compared to pupae immediately after injection.
source: Pupae injected with β−1,3-glucans (green dots) had increased relative abundances 2 days after injection compared to pupae immediately after injection, of (A) Tritriacontadiene, C33:2 (LMER: LR χ2 = x, df = 1, p=0.012) and (B) Tritriacontene, C33:1 (LR χ2 = 6.40, df = 1, p=0.046), but not (C) Pentatriacontadiene, C35:2 (LR χ2 = 1.56, df = 1, p=0.42) or (D) co-eluting Pentatriacontadiene and Pentatriacontene, C35:2 + C35:1 (LR χ2 = 0.25, df = 1, p=0.70).
evidence: This is supported by chemical analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Injection of β−1,3-glucans results in higher CHC abundance for two out of the four CHCs that were also specifically increased on Metarhizium-infected, unpacked pupae.
source: Hence, injection of β−1,3-glucans results in higher CHC abundance for two out of the four CHCs that were also specifically increased on Metarhizium-infected, unpacked pupae (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is supported by comparing the β-glucan injection results with the Metarhizium infection results.

claim: Some of the changes in pupal chemical profile can be directly linked to a host reaction to an immune elicitor.
source: These data reveal that some of the changes in pupal chemical profile can be directly linked to a host reaction to an immune elicitor, similar to findings in honeybees (Richard et al., 2012; Richard et al., 2008), mice (Arakawa et al., 2011) and humans (Shirasu and Touhara, 2011).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the β-glucan injection experiment results, with citations to similar findings in other species.

claim: Destructive disinfection significantly reduced the proportion of pupae that sporulated after 1 day by 65%.
source: Whilst 88% of pupae contracted infections, destructive disinfection significantly reduced the proportion of pupae that sporulated and hence became infectious (Figure 3A; GLM: LR χ2 = 40.47, df = 2, p<0.001; Tukey post-hoc comparisons: 1 vs. 5 d, p=0.04; all others, p<0.001). After only 1 day, the number of destructively disinfected pupae that sporulated decreased by 65%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: With more time (5 days), the ants could reduce the number of pupae sporulating by 95%.
source: With more time, the ants could reduce the number of pupae sporulating even further by 95%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Destructive disinfection permanently prevents pathogen replication.
source: Since the pupae were removed from the ants for fungal incubation, we can conclude that destructive disinfection permanently prevents pathogen replication.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental design where pupae were removed from ants before incubation.

claim: Smaller groups of ants (3 ants) were less efficient at destructive disinfection than larger ones (8 ants).
source: We repeated this experiment with a smaller number of ants (three ants per pupae per group) to investigate how group size influences the success of destructive disinfection. Smaller groups of ants were less efficient than larger ones: although they could still inhibit >90% of pupal infections within 5 days of unpacking, pupae tested for infection after 1 day still sporulated 70% of the time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; GLM: LR χ2 = 35.23, p<0.001; Tukey post-hoc comparisons: 0 vs. 1 day, p=0.2; 0 vs. 5 days, p<0.001; 1 vs. 5 days, p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: All three behaviours (unpacking, biting and poison spraying) must be performed in the correct order and interact to prevent pathogen replication.
source: We found that all three behaviours must be performed in the correct order and interact to prevent pathogen replication (overview graph showing odds ratios of sporulation in Figure 3B, full data dataset displayed in Figure 3—figure supplement 3; GLM: overall LR χ2 = 79.9, df = 5, p<0.001; interaction between behaviours LR χ2 = 20.6, df = 2, p<0.001; all post-hoc comparisons in Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The poison is the active antimicrobial compound that inhibits fungal growth.
source: As in sanitary care, the poison was the active antimicrobial compound that inhibited fungal growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Table 3, Tragust et al., 2013a; Graystock and Hughes, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The cocoon is hydrophobic and prevents the aqueous poison from reaching the pupae inside.
source: However, for the poison to function the pupae had to be removed from their cocoons and their cuticles damaged. Firstly, this is because the cocoon itself is hydrophobic and thus prevents the aqueous poison from reaching the pupae inside (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing pH differences in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The cuticle must be broken for the poison to enter the hemocoel of the pupae because the infection is growing internally at the time of unpacking.
source: Secondly, as the infection is growing internally at the time of unpacking, the cuticle must be broken in order for the poison to enter the hemocoel of the pupae. This is achieved with the perforations created by the ants biting the pupal cuticle.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that biting is necessary for poison effectiveness.

claim: The poison is probably the limiting factor determining whether destructive disinfection is successful.
source: As the active antimicrobial component, we concluded that the poison is probably the limiting factor determining whether destructive disinfection is successful.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing time and group size effects.

claim: The poison has a slow biosynthesis and each ant can only store a limited amount.
source: Because the poison has a slow biosynthesis and each ant can only store a limited amount (Tragust et al., 2013a; Hefetz and Blum, 1978), it would explain why destructive disinfection was more likely to be successful the longer the ants had to treat the pupae, and as the number of ants increased (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge from citations combined with inference from the experimental results.

claim: By sharing the task of poison synthesis and application, the ants probably increase their chances of preventing the pathogen becoming infectious.
source: By sharing the task of poison synthesis and application, the ants probably increase their chances of preventing the pathogen becoming infectious.
evidence: This is inferred from the group size effects observed in the experiments.

claim: Sporulating pupae were highly virulent and caused lethal infections that became contagious after host death in 42% of ants.
source: As in previous studies, sporulating corpses were highly virulent (Hughes et al., 2002; Loreto and Hughes, 2016) and caused lethal infections that became contagious after host death in 42% of ants (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claim: There was no disease transmission from destructively disinfected pupae.
source: However, there was no disease transmission from destructively disinfected pupae (Figure 4A; GLM: LR χ2 = 31.32, df = 1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: By preventing the pathogen from completing its lifecycle, destructive disinfection stops intra-colony disease transmission.
source: We therefore concluded that by preventing the pathogen from completing its lifecycle destructive disinfection stops intra-colony disease transmission (Figure 4B).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing no transmission from disinfected pupae.

claim: Ants do not only avoid, groom and isolate pathogens but can detect and eliminate infections developing inside the bodies of their nestmates, even before they have shown external disease symptoms.
source: These findings show that ants do not only avoid, groom and isolate pathogens (Cremer et al., 2007; Cremer et al., 2017) but can detect and eliminate infections developing inside the bodies of their nestmates, even before they have shown external disease symptoms.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The use of ant poison as an internal disinfectant within the body of others during destructive disinfection is a novel finding.
source: Whilst the role of ant poison as a topical disinfectant by ants and other animals (i.e. 'anting' behaviour in birds) is well characterised (Clayton et al., 2010; Verderane et al., 2007; Tragust, 2016), its use as an internal disinfectant within the body of others during destructive disinfection is a novel and a rare example of the kill-component of social immunity (Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
evidence: This claim contrasts the novel findings with established knowledge from citations.

claim: Eliminating infected kin to protect the rest of the group has been observed in termites and honeybees as well.
source: Eliminating infected kin to protect the rest of the group, observed in termites and honeybees as well (Rothenbuhler, 1964; Chouvenc and Su, 2012; Spivak and Gilliam, 1998), requires an unconditional level of altruism that is expected to be absent or at least rare in other forms of sociality (e.g. aggregations, non-superorganismal family groups and communal breeders [Cremer et al., 2017]), but has parallels to the immune system of the metazoan body (Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in other social insects.

claim: Both the immune system and social immunity have first lines of defences that reduce the risk of infection.
source: Both the immune system and social immunity have first lines of defences that reduce the risk of infection: pathogens that enter the body are met with mechanical and chemical defences, such as ciliated cells in the lung that move pathogens trapped in mucus out of the body (Cremer and Sixt, 2009), and in ants, sanitary care plays an analogous role (Tragust et al., 2013a; Graystock and Hughes, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis drawing on established knowledge from citations.

claim: If a pathogen circumvents first defences in the body and an infection occurs, the second line of defence is often a targeted elimination of the infected cells.
source: However, if a pathogen circumvents these first defences in the body and an infection occurs, the second line of defence is often a targeted elimination of the infected cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about immune system function.

claim: Immune cells detect an infection and transport cell death-inducing and antimicrobial compounds into infected cells by creating pores in their membrane.
source: This starts with immune cells detecting an infection and then transporting cell death-inducing and antimicrobial compounds into infected cells by creating pores in their membrane (Walch et al., 2014; Kägi et al., 1994; Chowdhury and Lieberman, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about immune cell function, supported by citations.

claim: Ants unpack infected pupae and make perforations in their cuticle, enabling them to spray poison directly into the pupae's body, displaying mechanisms analogous to immune cell elimination.
source: Likewise, our experiments revealed that ants unpack infected pupae and make perforations in their cuticle, enabling the ants to spray their poison directly into the pupae's body; hence they display mechanisms analogous to immune cell elimination.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the experimental findings and knowledge of immune function.

claim: The second line of defence destroys the infected cell/insect, along with the infection, to prevent transmission.
source: In both cases, this second line of defence destroys the infected cell/insect, along with the infection, to prevent transmission (Shore et al., 1976).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about immune and social immunity function, supported by citation.

claim: The loss of both somatic cells and individual insect workers can be tolerated with negligible effects on fitness.
source: Since the loss of both somatic cells and individual insect workers can be tolerated with negligible effects on fitness (Cremer and Sixt, 2009), these convergent strategies have likely evolved at both the multicellular and superorganismal levels of biological organisation, as an effective way to clear infections and avoid any further damage to the body and colony, respectively.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about fitness effects, supported by citation.

claim: These convergent strategies have likely evolved at both the multicellular and superorganismal levels of biological organisation as an effective way to clear infections.
source: Since the loss of both somatic cells and individual insect workers can be tolerated with negligible effects on fitness (Cremer and Sixt, 2009), these convergent strategies have likely evolved at both the multicellular and superorganismal levels of biological organisation, as an effective way to clear infections and avoid any further damage to the body and colony, respectively.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the convergent mechanisms observed.

claim: Evidence for ants using chemical information to rapidly and accurately target infected individuals has been lacking until this study.
source: Animals from a variety of taxa are known to identify sick conspecifics based on odour signals (Bozza, 2015; Poirotte et al., 2017; Kiesecker et al., 1999; Anderson and Behringer, 2013; Shirasu and Touhara, 2011; Swanson et al., 2009), and although it has been hypothesised that ants should also use chemical cues to detect sick colony members, evidence has so far been lacking (Ugelvig et al., 2010; Leclerc and Detrain, 2016; Bos et al., 2012). To our knowledge, we have therefore observed ants using chemical information for the first time to rapidly and accurately target infected individuals.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge and positions the current findings as novel, with citations.

claim: The chemical compounds with increased abundances on infected pupae are distinct from those that induce the removal of corpses in ants.
source: We found that the chemical compounds with increased abundances on infected pupae are distinct from those that induce the removal of corpses in ants (Diez et al., 2013; Qiu et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 1958), and, like in tapeworm-infected ants (Trabalon et al., 2000), are not pathogen-derived.
evidence: This is based on comparison with established knowledge from citations and the experimental data.

claim: The alteration of the hosts' chemical profile may arise during infection from the breakdown of hydrocarbons by Metarhizium penetration.
source: This alteration of the hosts' chemical profile may arise during infection from the breakdown of hydrocarbons by Metarhizium penetration (Lin et al., 2011) or after infection due to an immune response affecting the synthesis of specific hydrocarbons (Richard et al., 2012; Richard et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to relevant mechanisms.

claim: The alteration of the hosts' chemical profile may arise after infection due to an immune response affecting the synthesis of specific hydrocarbons.
source: This alteration of the hosts' chemical profile may arise during infection from the breakdown of hydrocarbons by Metarhizium penetration (Lin et al., 2011) or after infection due to an immune response affecting the synthesis of specific hydrocarbons (Richard et al., 2012; Richard et al., 2008). The latter is more likely because the ants only display destructive disinfection once the fungus is growing inside the pupae and injection of a fungal immune elicitor in the absence of live pathogen induced similar changes.
evidence: This is the preferred explanation based on the experimental data and citations.

claim: The four CHCs specifically increased on unpacked pupae are all long-chained CHCs (carbon chain length C33-35) with a low volatility.
source: The four CHCs specifically increased on unpacked pupae are all long-chained CHCs (carbon chain length C33-35) with a low volatility, meaning that the ants have to be close to or touching the pupae to detect them (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on chemical analysis data and knowledge of CHC properties from citation.

claim: Using low-volatility CHCs may be important so that the ants can accurately identify the infected pupae and do not mistakenly destroy healthy ones.
source: As ants keep pupae in large piles, using low-volatility CHCs may be important so that the ants can accurately identify the infected pupae and do not mistakenly destroy healthy ones.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of using low-volatility CHCs.

claim: Two of the four CHCs that were increased on infected pupae also had higher abundances on virus-infected honeybees or their brood when injected with a bacterial cell membrane component.
source: Interestingly, two of the four CHCs that were increased on infected pupae, as well as on pupae that were injected with the fungal cell wall component, also had higher abundances on virus-infected honeybees (Tritriacontadiene [Baracchi et al., 2012]), or their brood when injected with a bacterial cell membrane component (Tritriacontene [Richard et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is based on comparison with findings from cited studies in honeybees.

claim: These hydrocarbons may be evolutionarily conserved 'sickness cues' in Hymenopteran social insects.
source: This raises the possibility that these hydrocarbons are evolutionarily conserved 'sickness cues' in Hymenopteran social insects.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the similarity of CHC changes across different Hymenopteran species.

claim: Such cues may have evolved into general sickness signals in social insects as they alert their kin to the presence of a developing infection that will harm the colony if it spreads.
source: Such cues may have evolved into general sickness signals in social insects as they alert their kin to the presence of a developing infection that will harm the colony if it spreads (Shakhar and Shakhar, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary explanation supported by citation.

claim: Relying on cues generated by an immune response to detect infections is likely more robust and general than relying on pathogen-specific cues.
source: Relying on cues generated by an immune response to detect infections, over pathogen-specific cues, is likely more robust and general, similar to the expression of 'find-me/eat-me' signals by infected cells in vertebrate bodies (Ravichandran, 2010; Grimsley and Ravichandran, 2003), as well as the immune system responding to cell damage signals (danger signal hypothesis [Matzinger, 2007]).
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of immune-based cues, supported by citations to analogous systems.

claim: Altruistic displays of sickness can evolve in superorganisms, even if this results in the destruction of the individual that expresses them.
source: Such signals will be selected for in social insects because they can enhance colony fitness (and hence the indirect fitness of the sick individual) by preventing a systemic infection. Therefore, altruistic displays of sickness can evolve in superorganisms, even if this results in the destruction of the individual that expresses them (Cremer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the evolution of altruistic signaling, supported by citation.

claim: Destructive disinfection was highly effective and prevented 95% of infections becoming transmissible.
source: Our experiments show that destructive disinfection was highly effective and prevented 95% of infections becoming transmissible.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the study.

claim: Destructive disinfection will keep the average number of secondary infections caused by an initial infection low and the disease will die out within the colony.
source: Destructive disinfection will thus keep the average number of secondary infections caused by an initial infection low and the disease will die out within the colony (Schmid-Hempel, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about epidemiological consequences, supported by citation to disease ecology theory.

claim: Infections of Metarhizium and other generalist entomopathogenic fungi like Beauveria, though common in the field, do not seem to cause colony-wide epidemics in ants.
source: This may explain why infections of Metarhizium and other generalist entomopathogenic fungi like Beauveria, though common in the field (Reber et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2004a; Cremer et al., 2008; Keller et al., 2003), do not seem to cause colony-wide epidemics in ants (Cremer et al., 2017), but are more numerous in solitary species that lack social adaptations to resist disease (Roberts and St Leger, 2004; Shimazu, 1989; Lomer et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on field observations from citations.

claim: Behaviours like destructive disinfection that reduce pathogen fitness to zero could have selected for host manipulation in fungi that specialise on infecting ants.
source: Behaviours like destructive disinfection that are able to reduce pathogen fitness to zero could have selected for host manipulation in fungi that specialise on infecting ants, for example Ophiocordyceps and Pandora (Hughes et al., 2016; Loreto et al., 2014; Małagocka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary inference supported by citations.

claim: Specialist fungi manipulate their ant hosts into leaving the nest before they become infectious, possibly to avoid social immunity defences like destructive disinfection.
source: These fungi manipulate their ant hosts into leaving the nest before they become infectious and our study supports previous suggestions that this may be to avoid social immunity defences, like destructive disinfection, which would prevent them completing their lifecycle inside the nest (Loreto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by the current findings and citation to previous hypothesis.

claim: Generalist pathogens like Metarhizium are less likely to evolve strategies to escape social immunity defences because they infect a broad range of solitary and social hosts.
source: In contrast to specialists, generalist pathogens like Metarhizium infect a broad range of solitary and social hosts, making it less likely that they evolve strategies to escape social immunity defences (Cremer et al., 2017; Agosta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about pathogen evolution, supported by citations.

claim: Destructive disinfection has been observed in an unrelated supercolonial population of L. neglectus and another non-supercolonial/non-invasive Lasius species, L. niger.
source: We have also observed destructive disinfection in an unrelated supercolonial population of L. neglectus (Ugelvig et al., 2008) and another non-supercolonial/non-invasive Lasius species, L. niger (see Materials and methods for more information), suggesting that it may be a common behaviour that has evolved in Lasius, and possibly other ant genera, in response to the constant selection pressure applied by generalist pathogenic fungi (Cremer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on additional observations described in Materials and methods, with citations.

claim: Destructive disinfection may be a common behaviour that has evolved in Lasius, and possibly other ant genera, in response to the constant selection pressure applied by generalist pathogenic fungi.
source: We have also observed destructive disinfection in an unrelated supercolonial population of L. neglectus (Ugelvig et al., 2008) and another non-supercolonial/non-invasive Lasius species, L. niger (see Materials and methods for more information), suggesting that it may be a common behaviour that has evolved in Lasius, and possibly other ant genera, in response to the constant selection pressure applied by generalist pathogenic fungi (Cremer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations across multiple species, supported by citation.

claim: Destructive disinfection has probably evolved in ants because the removal of corpses from the colony alone does not guarantee that disease transmission is prevented.
source: Destructive disinfection has probably evolved in ants because the removal of corpses from the colony alone does not guarantee that disease transmission is prevented (Loreto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference supported by citation.

claim: Ants are usually sedentary, building nests that remain in the same location until the colony dies.
source: Ants are usually sedentary, building nests that remain in the same location until the colony dies (Boomsma et al., 2005; Schmid-Hempel, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ant ecology, supported by citations.

claim: Ants are highly territorial and forage mostly in the area around their nests, meaning that if they do not clear it of dead and potentially infectious nestmates, they are likely to be reencountered.
source: Additionally, they are highly territorial and forage mostly in the area around their nests, meaning that if they do not clear it of dead and potentially infectious nestmates, they are likely to be reencountered (Boomsma et al., 2005; Cremer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ant behavior, supported by citations.

claim: Ants tend to place corpses onto specific midden (trash) sites that are located inside or outside near the nest, but these sites are still regularly visited by midden workers.
source: Ants tend therefore to place corpses onto specific midden (trash) sites that are located inside or outside near the nest, but these sites are still regularly visited by midden workers (Verza et al., 2017; Hart and Ratnieks, 2002; Farji-Brener et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ant waste management, supported by citations.

claim: Although middens likely reduce a colony's exposure to corpses, they still represent a potential route for disease transmission back into the colony.
source: Consequently, although middens likely reduce a colony's exposure to corpses, they still represent a potential route for disease transmission back into the colony; hence the need to destroy infected corpses rather than simply taking them out of the nest.
evidence: This is an inference about disease risk based on ant behavior.

claim: In honeybees, corpses are dumped randomly outside of the hive, which is sufficient to prevent disease transmission because honeybees are unlikely to reencounter corpses whilst foraging on the wing.
source: This is in contrast to honeybees, where corpses are dumped randomly outside of the hive (Wilson-Rich et al., 2009). This behaviour is sufficient to prevent disease transmission because honeybees are unlikely to reencounter corpses whilst foraging on the wing (Spivak and Reuter, 2001).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about honeybee behavior, supported by citations.

claim: Termites cannibalise their dead, which is effective because the termite gut and/or its microbiome neutralises ingested pathogens.
source: Termites on the other hand cannibalise their dead (Chouvenc and Su, 2012; Rosengaus and Traniello, 2001). Cannibalism is effective because the termite gut and/or its microbiome neutralises ingested pathogens (Chouvenc et al., 2009; Rosengaus et al., 2014; Rosengaus et al., 1998) and has likely evolved because dead nestmates are a source of valuable nitrogen in their cellulose-base diet (Rosengaus et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about termite behavior, supported by citations.

claim: Cannibalism in termites has likely evolved because dead nestmates are a source of valuable nitrogen in their cellulose-base diet.
source: Cannibalism is effective because the termite gut and/or its microbiome neutralises ingested pathogens (Chouvenc et al., 2009; Rosengaus et al., 2014; Rosengaus et al., 1998) and has likely evolved because dead nestmates are a source of valuable nitrogen in their cellulose-base diet (Rosengaus et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference supported by citation.

claim: The same selective pressure has driven a suite of independently evolved innovations – the need to eliminate or remove infected individuals early in the infectious cycle.
source: The same selective pressure has driven this suite of independently evolved innovations – the need to eliminate or remove infected individuals early in the infectious cycle – with the ants expressing a particularly complex behavioural repertoire.
evidence: This is an inference about convergent evolution based on comparative analysis.

claim: Cells are rapidly detected and destroyed shortly after infection to prevent pathogen spread in multicellular organisms, which is a general principle in disease defence.
source: This seems to be a general principle in disease defence, as cells are also rapidly detected and destroyed shortly after infection to prevent pathogen spread in multicellular organisms (Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
evidence: This is a general principle supported by citation.

claim: Studying the similarities and differences between organismal immunity and social immunity could potentially lead to new insights about how disease defences evolve.
source: Studying the similarities and differences between organismal immunity and social immunity could therefore potentially lead to new insights about how disease defences evolve (Cremer and Sixt, 2009; Kennedy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about future research directions, supported by citations.

claim: In most social animals where relatedness is low or altruism is only conditionally expressed, disease defences tend to rely on self-protective infection avoidance, mutually expressed sanitary care and herd immunity only.
source: For example, in most social animals, where relatedness is low or altruism is only conditionally expressed (e.g. by young that eventually disperse to reproduce themselves), disease defences tend to rely on self-protective infection avoidance (Curtis, 2014), mutually expressed sanitary care (Nunn and Altizer, 2006) and herd immunity only (John and Samuel, 2000).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about disease defences in different social systems, supported by citations.

claim: Equivalent selection pressures during the major evolutionary transitions from unicellularity to multicellularity and from sociality to superorganismality have resulted in convergent defences that protect organisms and colonies from systemic disease spread.
source: In contrast, the results of our study suggest that equivalent selection pressures during the major evolutionary transitions from unicellularity to multicellularity in the metazoans, and from sociality to superorganismality in the social insects, have resulted in convergent defences that protect multicellular organisms and superorganismal insect societies from systemic disease spread, by ensuring the survival of the whole over its parts (Cremer and Sixt, 2009).
evidence: This is a broad evolutionary inference based on the study findings and citation.

claim: The invasive garden ant Lasius neglectus forms large, underground nests in the soil.
source: We studied the invasive garden ant Lasius neglectus (Cremer et al., 2008) that forms large, underground nests in the soil.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the study species, supported by citation.

claim: Populations of Lasius neglectus lack territorial structuring and instead consist of interconnected nests forming a single supercolony between which there is a constant exchanging of individual ants.
source: Populations of this species lack territorial structuring and instead consist of interconnected nests, forming a single supercolony between which there is a constant exchanging of individual ants (Cremer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the study species, supported by citation.

claim: Metarhizium brunneum is an obligately killing pathogen of Lasius ants.
source: As a model pathogen, we used an obligately killing pathogen of Lasius ants, Metarhizium brunneum (CDP unpublished data; strain MA275, KVL 03–143).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claim: Entomopathogenic Metarhizium fungi occur at high densities in the soil (up to 5000 conidiospores/g soil).
source: Entomopathogenic Metarhizium fungi occur at high densities in the soil (up to 5000 conidiospores/g soil [Keller et al., 2003]) and on sporulating cadavers (up to 12 million conidiospores/cadaver [Hughes et al., 2002, 2004b]) and are responsible for natural infections of ants in field populations (Reber et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2004a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Metarhizium ecology, supported by citations.

claim: Sporulating Metarhizium cadavers can contain up to 12 million conidiospores per cadaver.
source: Entomopathogenic Metarhizium fungi occur at high densities in the soil (up to 5000 conidiospores/g soil [Keller et al., 2003]) and on sporulating cadavers (up to 12 million conidiospores/cadaver [Hughes et al., 2002, 2004b]) and are responsible for natural infections of ants in field populations (Reber et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2004a).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Metarhizium, supported by citations.

claim: Metarhizium and other similar generalist fungi are responsible for natural infections of ants in field populations.
source: Entomopathogenic Metarhizium fungi occur at high densities in the soil (up to 5000 conidiospores/g soil [Keller et al., 2003]) and on sporulating cadavers (up to 12 million conidiospores/cadaver [Hughes et al., 2002, 2004b]) and are responsible for natural infections of ants in field populations (Reber et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2004a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Metarhizium and other similar generalist fungi are expected to have applied a persistent and pervasive selection pressure on ants over the course of their evolutionary history.
source: Metarhizium and other similar generalist fungi are therefore expected to have applied a persistent and pervasive selection pressure on ants over the course of their evolutionary history (Boomsma et al., 2005; Cremer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary history, supported by citations.

claim: The exposure procedure resulted in pupae receiving approximately 1800 conidiospores, of which 5% (approximately 95 conidiospores) passed through the cocoon and came into contact with the pupa inside.
source: This exposure procedure resulted in pupae receiving ~1800 conidiospores, of which 5% (~95 conidiospore) passed through the cocoon and came into contact with the pupa inside (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the time of unpacking, the majority of pupae were still alive.
source: At the time of unpacking, the majority of pupae were still alive (i.e. had an active dorsal aorta pulse; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and fungal outgrowth had not yet occurred (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on observational data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fungal outgrowth had not yet occurred at the time of unpacking.
source: At the time of unpacking, the majority of pupae were still alive (i.e. had an active dorsal aorta pulse; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and fungal outgrowth had not yet occurred (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on observational data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In the Jena population of L. neglectus, no control-treated pupae were destructively disinfected while >60% of pathogen-exposed pupae were destructively disinfected.
source: In both the Jena population and L. niger, no control-treated pupae were destructively disinfected (proportion ± 95% CIs: Jena = 0 ± 0–0.14; L. niger = 0 ± 0–0.16), whilst >60% of the pathogen-exposed pupae were destructively disinfected (proportion ± 95% CIs: Jena = 0.61 ± 0.41–0.78; L. niger = 0.95 ± 0.76–0.99).
evidence: This is based on observational data from additional experiments described in Materials and methods.

claim: In L. niger, no control-treated pupae were destructively disinfected while 95% of pathogen-exposed pupae were destructively disinfected.
source: In both the Jena population and L. niger, no control-treated pupae were destructively disinfected (proportion ± 95% CIs: Jena = 0 ± 0–0.14; L. niger = 0 ± 0–0.16), whilst >60% of the pathogen-exposed pupae were destructively disinfected (proportion ± 95% CIs: Jena = 0.61 ± 0.41–0.78; L. niger = 0.95 ± 0.76–0.99).
evidence: This is based on observational data from additional experiments described in Materials and methods.
